query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, high-temperature exposure in oxidizing environments accelerates a diffusion-driven decomposition of the metastable solid-solution state into Mg-rich intermetallic compounds that form primarily along grain boundaries and within the matrix. This intermetallic formation disrupts the integrity of the protective oxide film, leading to a measurable loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with a homogeneous distribution of Mg within the high-entropy alloy matrix.
generation.intervention: Controlled high-temperature heat treatment under oxidizing conditions (with a complementary non-oxidizing/inert condition as a controlled comparison).
generation.conditions: Service-regime temperatures in the range of approximately 600–800 °C applied for durations (e.g., 10–50 hours) sufficient to allow diffusion-driven phase separation, with one group exposed to oxidizing atmospheres and a parallel group to inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds, especially along grain boundaries, which leads to the breakdown of a coherent, protective oxide film.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion of Mg atoms results in its segregation and the formation of intermetallic phases. In oxidizing environments, this process is accelerated as the formation of oxide scales further drives local compositional gradients, thereby facilitating the coarsening and networking of Mg-rich intermetallic phases that compromise the corrosion and oxidation resistance of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial metastable solid-solution state, samples exposed to high-temperature oxidizing conditions will develop a more continuous network of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds and exhibit a significant decrease in both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation protection. In contrast, samples treated under inert conditions will show a slower or less pronounced transformation, retaining more of the original protective properties.
generation.baseline: The microstructural state and corrosion/oxidation resistance of the as-cast or as-processed metastable solid-solution alloy.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within the specified temperature range (600–800 °C) and exposure durations (10–50 hours). Outside this envelope—in lower temperatures or very short exposures—the kinetics might be insufficient for appreciable Mg segregation and intermetallic formation as described.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of intermetallic evolution and the spatial distribution of Mg-rich phases remain to be precisely quantified and may vary with minor elemental additions or slight compositional differences. The exact threshold conditions for the transition in corrosion behavior are also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples in the identical as-solid-solution state. Subject one set to high-temperature treatment (600–800 °C for 10–50 hours) in an oxidizing environment and the other set to the same thermal profile under an inert atmosphere. Post-treatment, assess the microstructural evolution via TEM/SEM and composition via EDS, and evaluate corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance using standardized tests (e.g., salt spray testing, high-temperature oxidation weight gain).
measurements: Quantitative phase analysis and imaging of intermetallic formation (e.g., via TEM, SEM, and XRD)
Distribution and connectivity of Mg-rich intermetallic phases (via EDS mapping)
Corrosion resistance metrics (exposure tests, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
High-temperature oxidation resistance (e.g., weight gain measurements and oxide scale integrity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the oxidizing-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the formation of contiguous Mg-rich intermetallic compounds and a corresponding degradation in corrosion/oxidation resistance as compared to both the initial state and samples treated in an inert atmosphere.
